questions.stem: Katie, 28, is in ED with 4 days of progressive weakness in both legs. On examination her legs are spastic, and pinprick is reduced from both feet up to the tops of both thighs. Her arms are normal. What should you do next in the sensory examination?
options: Do Romberg's test to confirm a dorsal column sensory deficit
Test pinprick up the trunk from the groin towards the nipples to find a level
Compare each leg dermatome with the other side to find a single affected root
Test two-point discrimination on both soles to grade the sensory loss
questions.why: When sensation is abnormal throughout both legs, keep testing up the trunk to find a sensory level. Useful landmarks are L1 at the inguinal ligament, T10 at the umbilicus and T4 at the nipples. A truncal level puts the lesion in the spinal cord and tells you which part of the spine to image.
notes: Katie cannot stand, so Romberg's test is unsafe and impossible here. It also would not help localise the lesion.
Loss in both legs together with spasticity points to a cord lesion, not a single root, so comparing dermatomes side to side misses the key finding.
Grading loss on the soles adds nothing to localisation. The step that matters is finding the upper border of the sensory loss on the trunk.

questions.stem: Katie, 28, has a short, enhancing intramedullary lesion at T7-T8 on MRI. Nothing is compressing the cord. She is afebrile, and her CRP and white cell count are normal. Neurology agree this is an acute demyelinating myelitis. Her sensory level is rising. What is the first-line acute treatment?
options: Oral prednisolone 50 mg daily for 5 days, then taper over 2 weeks
IV immunoglobulin 2 g/kg divided over 5 days
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days
IV dexamethasone 10 mg stat, then 4 mg orally 6-hourly
questions.why: Once compression and infection have been excluded, an acute demyelinating relapse is treated with high-dose IV methylprednisolone, 1 g daily for 3 to 5 days, on neurology advice. Monitor her blood glucose while she is on it. Plasma exchange is the next step if she does not respond.
notes: A low-dose oral steroid course is not the standard treatment for an acute, disabling myelitis. High-dose pulsed methylprednisolone is used.
IVIG is not first-line for MS-related myelitis. If steroids fail, the escalation is plasma exchange.
This dexamethasone regimen is used for malignant spinal cord compression, and the MRI has excluded compression.

questions.stem: Katie, 28, has an enhancing demyelinating lesion in her thoracic cord. She asks how inflammation can stop her legs working when nothing is pressing on the cord. Her weakness is spastic, with brisk reflexes and no wasting. What best explains her acute weakness?
options: Loss of myelin abolishes saltatory conduction, causing conduction block in tracts
Inflammation destroys anterior horn cells, denervating the leg muscles
Cord swelling occludes the anterior spinal artery, infarcting the cord
Antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction
questions.why: Myelin lets the action potential jump from node to node (saltatory conduction). In an inflamed, demyelinated segment the current leaks away and conduction slows or fails, which blocks the descending corticospinal signals. Function can return as inflammation settles, sodium channels redistribute along the axon and remyelination occurs.
notes: Loss of anterior horn cells gives lower motor neuron signs (flaccidity, wasting, areflexia), not the spasticity and brisk reflexes Katie has.
Anterior spinal artery infarction is sudden, spares the dorsal columns and is not an enhancing demyelinating plaque. Katie's dorsal column loss is the most prominent deficit.
A neuromuscular junction disorder causes fatigable weakness with normal reflexes and no sensory level, sphincter problems or upper motor neuron signs.

questions.stem: Katie's right leg is weaker and more spastic than her left, but her pinprick loss is worse on the left. MRI shows an eccentric right dorsolateral lesion at the T7-T8 vertebral level. Which feature of the pain and temperature pathway explains why her pinprick loss is worse on the side opposite the lesion?
options: They ascend ipsilaterally in the dorsal columns and cross in the medulla
They ascend uncrossed in the spinothalamic tract and cross in the thalamus
They cross at the pyramidal decussation alongside the corticospinal fibres
They cross in the anterior white commissure within one or two segments of entry
questions.why: Pain and temperature fibres synapse in the dorsal horn, then cross in the anterior white commissure within one or two segments and ascend in the contralateral spinothalamic tract. A right-sided cord lesion therefore reduces pinprick on the left, while corticospinal and dorsal column deficits stay on the right.
notes: Fine touch, vibration and proprioception take this route (dorsal columns, crossing in the medulla). Pain and temperature fibres cross in the cord.
The spinothalamic tract already carries crossed fibres. Crossing happens in the cord, not the thalamus, which is why a cord lesion gives a contralateral deficit.
The pyramidal decussation is a motor crossing for corticospinal fibres. It explains why her weakness is on the same side as the lesion, not why her pinprick loss is opposite.
